kept.fix: Normalise the alias where the symbol is chosen: `let symbolName = shortcut == "esc" ? "escape" : shortcut` and test `systemIcons.contains(symbolName)` / `Image(systemName: symbolName)`. One line, and the existing call sites stay as they are.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: OraButton.swift:141 tests the shortcut string against a list containing "escape", and every Cancel call site passes "esc" (DialogView.swift:45, BookmarkEditDialog.swift:20 and 60, ExtensionStoreCards.swift:454, DownloadCollisionDialog.swift:45, NewContainerButton.swift:85, EditContainerModal.swift:74), so the Cancel chip falls into the Text branch at 148 while the neighbouring Confirm renders the SF Symbol.

kept.title: Password autofill key button has no accessible name
kept.evidence: `PasswordAutofillTriggerView.body` wraps `Image(systemName: "key.fill")` in a `Button` (lines 142-165) with no `.help` and no `.accessibilityLabel`; the file has no accessibility modifiers at all. The suggestion rows below it (`PasswordSuggestionButton`, lines 185-222) also rely on their visual content only, so the "Use Strong Password" and saved-credential rows read as loose text fragments.
kept.user_impact: The badge that offers a saved password inside a form field announces itself as "key.fill", and there is no tooltip explaining what the badge in the field does.
kept.fix: Add `.help("Autofill password")` and `.accessibilityLabel(Text("Autofill password"))` to the trigger button, and `.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` plus `.accessibilityAddTraits(isSelected ? [.isButton, .isSelected] : .isButton)` on `PasswordSuggestionButton`'s label content.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: PasswordAutofillTriggerView (PasswordAutofillOverlayView.swift:140-169) wraps Image(systemName: "key.fill") in a Button with no help or label, and PasswordSuggestionButton (184-221) builds its row from a favicon, caller content and an accessory symbol with no combined element or selected trait; the file contains no accessibility modifier at all.

kept.title: Sidebar section titles are plain text, so the VoiceOver rotor has no headings
kept.evidence: `PinnedTabsList` draws `Text("Pinned")` styled as a section title (lines 20-24) with no `.accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader)`; `grep -rn accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader)` and `accessibilityRotor` return nothing in the repo. The sidebar's other landmarks (favourites grid, space header, tab list, bottom widget row) are likewise unlabelled containers in `SidebarView.spacesContent` (lines 256-345).
kept.user_impact: A VoiceOver user has to swipe through every tab to get from the pinned section to the normal one; the heading rotor, the usual way to jump between sidebar sections, is empty.
kept.fix: NormalTabsList has no title at all (grep for `Text(` in that file returns nothing), so there is no equivalent heading to mark and it should come off files_to_touch. Keep the change to PinnedTabsList.swift: `.accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader)` on the "Pinned" title. If the normal list needs a landmark, that belongs on the container in SidebarView.spacesContent, not in NormalTabsList.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed for PinnedTabsList: Text("Pinned") at lines 19-23 is styled as a section title with no header trait, and grep finds no accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader) or accessibilityRotor anywhere in the repo.

kept.title: Tab switcher previews are focusable but announce only a screenshot
kept.evidence: `tabPreviewItem` makes each card `.focusable()` and binds it to `@FocusState private var focusedTab` (lines 108-113), and `tabPreview` activates on tap (line 130-132), but neither carries a label. The card's content is `Image(nsImage: snapshot.image)` (line 138) plus a title bar rendered only for the focused card (line 119-121), so an unfocused card exposes nothing but an unnamed image, and `.focusEffectDisabled()` (line 94) removes the system focus ring.
kept.user_impact: Ctrl+Tab is the fastest way to switch tabs, and with VoiceOver it reads as a row of unnamed images with no indication of which one is selected.
kept.fix: Attach the modifiers to `tabPreview(for:)`, where the tap action lives, rather than to `tabPreviewItem`, and add `.accessibilityAction { activateTab(tab) }` so VoiceOver can pick a card: `.focusable()` alone does not make the row's `.onTapGesture` (line 128-130) reachable.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: tabPreviewItem (FloatingTabSwitcher.swift:107-112) is .focusable()/.focused with no label; the card content is Image(nsImage:) (135-140) or a blank rounded rectangle, and the title bar renders only for the focused card (117-119), so unfocused cards expose an unnamed image. .focusEffectDisabled() at line 94 removes the system ring, though the code does draw its own focusBorder.

kept.title: Dialogs shown through DialogManager.show print a "return" chip that Return never triggers
kept.evidence: OraButton renders the shortcut only as a decoration: its body (aura/Shared/Components/Buttons/OraButton.swift:120-171) draws the chip but never calls `.keyboardShortcut`. The only place Return is wired is OraRoot.swift:269, `if event.keyCode == 36, let onConfirm = dialogManager.dialogs.last?.onConfirm`, and `onConfirm` is set only by `DialogManager.confirm` (DialogManager.swift:79-81), never by `DialogManager.show` (12-18). DownloadCollisionDialog is presented through `show` (DownloadManager.swift:335-346) and ExtensionConsentSheet through `show` (ExtensionStoreCards.swift:487-497); neither contains a text field, so there is no onSubmit fallback either (unlike BookmarkEditDialog, whose OraInput carries onSubmit at BookmarkEditDialog.swift:17-18).
kept.user_impact: A download name collision or an extension install prompt shows a Return chip on the primary button, and pressing Return does nothing: the download sits blocked on WebKit's destination callback until the user reaches for the mouse. Escape works, so the only key the dialog advertises as "yes" is the one that is dead.
kept.fix: Bind the key where the chip is drawn, in OraButton: after `.disabled(isDisabled)` add `.keyboardShortcut(keyboardShortcut == "return" ? .defaultAction : keyboardShortcut == "esc" ? .cancelAction : nil)` (guarding nil by branching, since keyboardShortcut takes no optional). Dialogs opened through `confirm` are unaffected because OraRoot's monitor consumes Return before SwiftUI sees it, and the buttons that show no chip gain nothing.

kept.title: ShareLinkButton is dead code
kept.evidence: `grep -rn "ShareLinkButton" --include="*.swift" aura` returns only the declaration in this file. Nothing constructs it, and it carries the NSViewRepresentable `ShareSourceView` (lines 30-45) with it. It is also the only URLBarButton use in the tree with no `.oraShortcutHelp`, so if it were ever mounted it would be the one unlabelled toolbar glyph.
kept.user_impact: None at runtime; it is 45 lines of unreferenced chrome that a reader has to check against the real toolbar before concluding sharing is unimplemented.
kept.fix: Delete the file. If sharing is planned, the button belongs next to the other TopToolbar entries with `.oraShortcutHelp("Share", ...)` like every sibling.

dropped.title: The space actions button only takes clicks while the pointer hovers it
dropped.reason: Refuted as an a11y bug. `.allowsHitTesting(false)` (SpaceHeaderRow.swift:135) suppresses pointer hit-testing; it does not remove the Button from the accessibility tree, and VoiceOver activates a SwiftUI Button through its accessibility action, not a synthesised click, so "cannot be reached by keyboard or VoiceOver at all" is not established from the code. The comparison with TabItem is also not evidence of a defect: TabItem's comment (135-138) explains a close-button-specific bug where a row slides under a stationary pointer after a close, which does not apply to a space header that never moves under the pointer. Deleting line 135 as proposed would make an invisible ellipsis button swallow clicks on the row's trailing edge, a real regression. Dropping.

windows-chrome.summary: The chrome is genuinely custom (hidden titlebar, hand-placed native traffic lights, explicit drag regions, hover-revealed rows) and most of it is carefully reasoned, but the traffic-light story falls apart in three reachable configurations: a second window, a right-hand sidebar with the toolbar hidden, and a hover-revealed toolbar over an open sidebar panel. Menu commands all address NSApp.keyWindow with no fallback to the owning browser window, which is a plausible cause of the reported dead ⌘T, and the File menu's Close Window item is bound to a stale enabled state that never fires. The rest is smaller: the paint probe orders two real top-level windows on screen at first page load, the custom window buttons are invisible to VoiceOver and the keyboard, and NSWindow+Extensions plus the pre-macOS-15 drag backport are dead weight.

kept.title: Second window loses its traffic lights when another window hides its toolbar
kept.evidence: `@AppStorage("ui.toolbar.hidden") private var isToolbarHidden: Bool = false` is a global default, while `ToolbarManager` is created per window in `OraRoot` and writes that same key in `didSet` (ToolbarManager.swift:15). Line 168 mixes them: `let rowIsUp = !isToolbarHidden || toolbarManager.isFloatingToolbarVisible`, then line 172 hides the native buttons. `BrowserView.isToolbarRowUp` (BrowserView.swift:112) uses only `toolbarManager.isToolbarHidden`.
kept.user_impact: With two windows open, hiding the toolbar in window A flips the shared default; window B keeps drawing its toolbar row (its own manager still says visible) but its close/minimise/zoom buttons vanish, leaving an empty 78pt gap where they should be. The only way back is to unhide the toolbar in window A.
kept.fix: The proposed one-line fix is right. While in there, note the expression `!isToolbarHidden || isFloatingToolbarVisible` now exists in four places (WindowAccessor:168, BrowserView:113, BrowserContentContainer:26, inverted in SidebarView:261). A `var isRowUp: Bool { !isToolbarHidden || isFloatingToolbarVisible }` on ToolbarManager and four call sites reading it is the same size of diff and stops the next drift.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. ToolbarManager is @State in OraRoot (OraRoot.swift:43), so one per window, and its didSet writes "ui.toolbar.hidden" (ToolbarManager.swift:15). WindowAccessor.swift:9 reads that same key through @AppStorage, which re-renders on any in-process write, while BrowserView.isToolbarRowUp (BrowserView.swift:113) and BrowserContentContainer (line 26) read the per-window manager. Window B therefore keeps drawing its toolbar row with its native buttons hidden, and SidebarHeader will not draw stand-ins because its own manager still says the toolbar is visible.

kept.title: Menu commands post to NSApp.keyWindow, so ⌘T and friends die while a utility window or popover is key
kept.evidence: Every command posts at the key window: `NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .showLauncher, object: NSApp.keyWindow)`. `OraRoot` claims `.showLauncher` with scope `.windowOrKey`, whose rule is `sender === window ?? keyWindow` (OraRoot.swift:332). When the Passwords window (PasswordsWindow.swift:51) or a WebKit extension popover is key, the sender is a window no `OraRoot` owns, so no window claims the post and nothing happens. `EdgeRevealView.isCoveredByPanel` (GlobalMouseTrackingArea.swift:134) confirms child panels do become key.
kept.user_impact: This is the reported "sometimes ⌘T does not open the launcher": press ⌘T after clicking an extension popup or with the Passwords window in front and the keystroke is swallowed silently. Close Tab, Find, Reload and the zoom commands drop the same way.
kept.fix: Keep the helper, but make the resolved window key before posting when it is not already: `let target = AppDelegate.commandTarget; if target !== NSApp.keyWindow { target?.makeKeyAndOrderFront(nil) }; NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .showLauncher, object: target)`. Without that, ⌘T from the Passwords window opens the launcher in a background window whose text field cannot take first responder, which is the second half of the reported symptom (launcher up, caret nowhere).
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed on both paths. Every command posts `object: NSApp.keyWindow` and `.windowOrKey` resolves `sender === window ?? keyWindow` (OraRoot.swift:332-336), so a post whose sender is a window no OraRoot owns is claimed by nobody. PasswordsWindow.swift:38-54 makes a real key NSWindow, and extension popups are shown with a transient NSPopover (ExtensionControllerDelegate.swift:271-279), whose window becomes key and is a child of the browser window (the same assumption EdgeRevealView.isCoveredByPanel relies on, GlobalMouseTrackingArea.swift:132-135).

kept.title: No window controls at all with the sidebar on the right and the toolbar hidden
kept.evidence: `if sidebarManager.sidebarPosition != .secondary, !appState.isFullscreen { WindowControls(...) }` — the stand-in controls only render for a leading sidebar. Meanwhile `WindowAccessor.updateTrafficLights` hides the native buttons whenever the toolbar row is down (`button.isHidden = !(isFullscreen || showInToolbar)`, WindowAccessor.swift:172).
kept.user_impact: Move the sidebar to the right and hide the toolbar, and the window has no close, minimise or zoom button anywhere: native ones hidden, stand-ins not drawn. The window can only be closed from the Dock or by quitting.
kept.fix: The proposed fix is wrong: with the sidebar on the right, SidebarHeader sits on the right edge, so leading-aligned stand-ins would land at the far right of the window, nowhere near where the native buttons live. Fix it in WindowAccessor instead, where the hiding decision is made: it already pulls ToolbarManager out of the environment, and OraRoot injects SidebarManager the same way (OraRoot.swift:182), so add `@Environment(SidebarManager.self) private var sidebarManager` and hide the native buttons only when a stand-in will be drawn: `let standInDraws = sidebarManager.sidebarPosition != .secondary; button.isHidden = !(isFullscreen || showInToolbar || !standInDraws)`. With the sidebar on the right the native buttons then stay at their default titlebar origins over the content pane, which is where a right-sidebar layout wants them.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. WindowAccessor.swift:168-173 hides the native buttons whenever the row is down, and the only four WindowControls call sites (SidebarHeader.swift:23, HistoryPanelView.swift:66, FilesPanelView.swift:37, DownloadsHistoryView.swift:38) all gate on `sidebarPosition != .secondary`. Right sidebar plus hidden toolbar leaves no close/minimise/zoom anywhere, and Close Window is broken too (windows-chrome-5), so the window really is stuck.

kept.title: Close Window never fires, and the customisable ⇧⌘W shortcut is wired to nothing
kept.evidence: The item is `.keyboardShortcut("w", modifiers: .command)` and `.disabled({ guard let keyWindow = NSApp.keyWindow else { return true }; return !["Settings", "Passwords"].contains(keyWindow.title) }())`. That closure runs when the commands body is built, not when the key window changes. "Close Tab" sits above it with the same ⌘W equivalent and is never disabled, so it wins the key-equivalent search and posts `.closeActiveTab` at the Passwords window, which no `OraRoot` claims. `KeyboardShortcuts.Window.close` (⇧⌘W, KeyboardShortcuts.swift:180) is listed in the customisable set at line 385 but no menu item uses it. "Settings" is stale too: settings is a tab now (TabManager.swift:509), not a window.
kept.user_impact: ⌘W in the Passwords window does nothing, the File menu shows a permanently greyed "Close Window", and the Close Window shortcut the user can rebind in Settings has no effect anywhere.
kept.fix: Fix stands. Window.fullscreen (⌃⌘F) is dead in exactly the same way and belongs in the same edit: either add a menu item that calls `NSApp.keyWindow?.toggleFullScreen(nil)` or drop it from allShortcuts, so Settings stops advertising a shortcut that does nothing.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. OraCommands.swift:52-61 gives Close Window a hardcoded ⌘W that Close Tab (line 50) already owns higher in the same menu, and the `.disabled` value is computed when the commands body is evaluated, not when the key window changes. KeyboardShortcuts.Window.close (⇧⌘W) and Window.fullscreen are both listed in allShortcuts (KeyboardShortcuts.swift:385) and neither id appears at any other call site, so both are rebindable in Settings and wired to nothing. The "Settings" title check is stale: settings opens as a tab.

kept.title: Sidebar panels draw a second set of traffic lights while the toolbar is hover-revealed
kept.evidence: `if sidebarManager.sidebarPosition != .secondary, toolbarManager.isToolbarHidden { WindowControls(...) }` — the same two-line condition and comment are copy-pasted into FilesPanelView.swift:36 and DownloadsHistoryView.swift:37. `SidebarHeader`'s call site in SidebarView.swift:261 adds the missing term: `toolbarManager.isToolbarHidden, !toolbarManager.isFloatingToolbarVisible`.
kept.user_impact: With the toolbar hidden and the history, files or downloads panel open, moving the pointer to the top edge reveals the toolbar with its native traffic lights while the panel header keeps drawing its own set right below them: two rows of close buttons at once.
kept.fix: Put the shared term on ToolbarManager rather than on WindowControls, since BrowserView, BrowserContentContainer and WindowAccessor need the same expression (see windows-chrome-1): `var isRowUp: Bool { !isToolbarHidden || isFloatingToolbarVisible }`, then the three panel headers and SidebarView.spacesContent read `!toolbarManager.isRowUp`. files_to_touch becomes ToolbarManager.swift plus the four views, not WindowControls.swift.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed by reading all four call sites. SidebarView.swift:261 gates on `isToolbarHidden && !isFloatingToolbarVisible`; HistoryPanelView.swift:65, FilesPanelView.swift:35 and DownloadsHistoryView.swift:37 drop the second term, so a hover-revealed toolbar row (which brings the native buttons back, WindowAccessor.swift:169-172) is drawn at the same time as the panel's stand-ins.

kept.title: Custom window buttons are invisible to VoiceOver and unreachable by keyboard
kept.evidence: `Image(imageName)...onTapGesture { performAction() }`. No `Button`, no `accessibilityLabel`, no `help`, no `.accessibilityAddTraits(.isButton)`, and no hover cursor. The native buttons these stand in for carry all of that for free, and they are hidden exactly when this view renders (WindowAccessor.swift:172).
kept.user_impact: With the toolbar hidden, VoiceOver announces nothing for the three controls, Full Keyboard Access cannot reach them, and there is no tooltip. The rest of the chrome uses `URLBarButton` with `oraShortcutHelp`, so this row is the odd one out.
kept.fix: Fix stands. Match the codebase's own words: the zoom control calls toggleFullScreen(nil), so label it "Full Screen" rather than "Zoom", and keep .help identical to the accessibility label.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. WindowControlButton.body is a bare Image with .onTapGesture (WindowControls.swift:64-85): no Button, no accessibility label or trait, no .help, no cursor. These are the only controls on screen while the toolbar is hidden, because WindowAccessor hides the native ones exactly then, and every other chrome control in the codebase goes through URLBarButton with .oraShortcutHelp.

kept.title: Double-click on chrome does two different things, and neither honours the system setting
kept.evidence: The toolbar drag region does `if event.clickCount == 2 { window?.performZoom(nil) }`, while a double-click on the sidebar background calls `toggleMaximizeWindow()` (SidebarView.swift:342) which routes to the hand-written `NSWindow.toggleMaximized()` (NSWindow+Extensions.swift:27) that sets the frame to `screen.visibleFrame`. Neither reads `AppleActionOnDoubleClick`, which the real titlebar honours (Zoom, Minimize, Fill, None).
kept.user_impact: Double-clicking the toolbar zooms, double-clicking the sidebar fills the visible frame with a different animation, and users who set double-click to Minimise or Do Nothing get neither.
kept.fix: The switch needs the real value set: macOS writes "Minimize", "Maximize", "Fill" or "None" to AppleActionOnDoubleClick in NSGlobalDomain, and the key is absent by default. So: nil or "Maximize" -> performZoom(nil), "Minimize" -> performMiniaturize(nil), "Fill" -> the existing toggleMaximized() (that is what fill means), "None" -> return. Do not delete toggleMaximized; the Fill case is its one remaining caller.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: WindowDragHandle.swift:11-12 calls performZoom on a double click, SidebarView.swift:342 routes a double click on the sidebar background to NSWindow.toggleMaximized (NSWindow+Extensions.swift:27) which animates to screen.visibleFrame instead. Neither reads AppleActionOnDoubleClick. Downgraded from medium: the two regions are visually distinct surfaces and the mismatch costs a user nothing but a slightly different animation; only the minority who changed the system setting get the wrong action.

kept.title: NSWindow+Extensions is mostly dead code with what-not-why comments
kept.evidence: `maximize()` (line 81) and `restoreToDefaultSize()` (line 95) have no callers anywhere in the repo; only `toggleMaximized()` is used, once, from SidebarView.swift:375. `toggleMaximized` also re-implements the `isMaximized` property inline (lines 35 to 38 duplicate lines 73 to 76), and the comments narrate the code ("Get the screen's visible frame", "Store the current frame before maximizing", "Maximize to fill the visible screen area").
kept.user_impact: None directly; 112 lines of window code where about 15 are live, and the duplicated tolerance check is the kind of thing that drifts.
kept.fix: Delete maximize() and restoreToDefaultSize(), then fold `isMaximized` into toggleMaximized as its only caller (a property with one call site inside the same file is the same amount of code either way, but do not leave both copies of the tolerance check).
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed by grep: maximize() and restoreToDefaultSize() have no callers in aura or auraTests, the isMaximized property is read only by maximize(), and toggleMaximized re-implements the same tolerance check inline at lines 35-38. The comments do narrate the code.

kept.title: Dead pre-macOS-15 window drag backport
kept.evidence: `if #available(macOS 15.0, *) { content.gesture(WindowDragGesture(), including: mask) } else { content.gesture(BackportWindowDragGesture(...)) }` with `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 15.0` and `LSMinimumSystemVersion 15.0`. `BackportWindowDragGesture` (lines 188 to 214) can never run, and it carries filler comments ("Makes intent cleaner, if we're dragging, then just return", "Maybe some other case needs to be watched for here").
kept.user_impact: None at runtime; an unreachable gesture type plus its `isDragging` binding and the `@State var isDragging` at line 18 that exists only to feed it.
kept.fix: Collapse the modifier to `content.gesture(WindowDragGesture(), including: mask)`, delete `BackportWindowDragGesture`, the `isDragging` binding on `OraWindowDragGesture` and `@State var isDragging` in `ContainerView`.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 15.0 in every build config, so the #available(macOS 15.0) else branch at ContainerView.swift:182 is unreachable. `isDragging` is written by nothing: line 174's mask term is permanently false and line 80 only passes the binding through, so deleting it changes no behaviour.

kept.title: WindowReader schedules a main-queue block and rewrites @State on every SwiftUI update
kept.evidence: `func updateNSView(...) { DispatchQueue.main.async { [weak nsView] in if let win = nsView?.window { self.window = win } } }` — unconditional, with no check that the window actually changed. `OraRoot` re-runs its body on every tab, toolbar and theme change, and each pass writes the binding again, which feeds `onChange(of: window)` in OraRoot.swift:194.
kept.user_impact: A dispatch hop plus a state write per body pass, in the window that hosts everything. Not visible on its own, but pure churn on the hottest view in the app.
kept.fix: Guard on the value: `if let win = nsView?.window, win !== self.window { self.window = win }`, and do the same in `makeNSView`.
kept.verify_reason: The code is as described (WindowReader.swift:15-19 dispatches and assigns unconditionally on every update) and the guard is strictly cheaper. Kept at low with reduced confidence: I could not verify from the code whether SwiftUI's @State setter dedupes an equal NSWindow? value, and if it does the current cost is one dispatch hop per body pass rather than a re-render storm. The fix is correct either way and cannot regress anything, since the only consumer is `onChange(of: window)` in OraRoot.swift:192, which already fires on change only.

kept.title: Missing applicationSupportsSecureRestorableState, so macOS disables state restoration
kept.evidence: `AppDelegate` implements `applicationDidFinishLaunching`, `applicationShouldTerminate`, `applicationWillTerminate`, `application(_:open:)` and `applicationShouldHandleReopen`, but not `applicationSupportsSecureRestorableState`; the selector appears nowhere in the repo and Info.plist sets no restoration keys.
kept.user_impact: macOS logs "Secure coding is not enabled for restorable state" on every launch and opts the app out of window state restoration, so scene windows fall back to their `.defaultSize(1440x900)` more often than they should.
kept.fix: Add one method to `AppDelegate`: `func applicationSupportsSecureRestorableState(_ app: NSApplication) -> Bool { true }`.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: AppDelegate (OraApp.swift:6-123) implements five delegate methods and not applicationSupportsSecureRestorableState, and the selector appears nowhere in the repo. NSApplication's default answer is false, which logs the secure-coding warning at every launch and opts the app out of restorable state.

kept.title: Factory-made windows all open dead centre with no cascade
kept.evidence: `let unplaced = window.frame; window.setFrameAutosaveName("AuraBrowserWindow"); if window.frame == unplaced { window.center() }` — only the first window claims the autosave name, so every later one centres on the same rect. `openWindow(with:)` is the path used by external links (OraApp.swift:110), the privacy settings link and the page context menu.
kept.user_impact: Open two links from another app with "open in a new window" set and the second window lands exactly on top of the first, hiding it completely.
kept.fix: The proposed call is backwards: `cascadeTopLeft(from:)` moves the receiver, so calling it on `front` would shove the existing window. Cascade the new window instead: `if let front = AppDelegate.browserWindow(in: NSApp.orderedWindows) { window.cascadeTopLeft(from: NSPoint(x: front.frame.minX, y: front.frame.maxY)) } else { window.center() }`, still inside the `window.frame == unplaced` branch.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. WindowFactory.swift:35-37: only the first window to claim "AuraBrowserWindow" gets a restored frame; every later one keeps the unplaced frame and is centred, so two externally opened links land on the identical rect. Reached from AppDelegate.handleIncomingURLs when externalLinkTarget == .newWindow (OraApp.swift:108-112).

kept.title: WindowControls re-checks isFullscreen its callers already checked and returns an explicit EmptyView
kept.evidence: `if !isFullscreen { HStack { ... } } else { EmptyView() }` inside a `ViewBuilder` body, while `SidebarHeader.swift:22` already guards `!appState.isFullscreen` before constructing it and still passes `isFullscreen: appState.isFullscreen`. The three panel headers pass the same flag without the outer guard, so the rule lives in four places.
kept.user_impact: None visible; the same condition is spelled three different ways across four call sites, which is how windows-chrome-3 and windows-chrome-6 drifted apart in the first place.
kept.fix: Do the `else { EmptyView() }` deletion here. Leave removing the isFullscreen parameter to whichever of findings 3 and 6 lands first, so the condition ends up in one place (ToolbarManager.isRowUp plus AppState.isFullscreen read from the environment) rather than being churned twice.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: WindowControls.swift:13-27 has the explicit `else { EmptyView() }` inside a ViewBuilder, and SidebarHeader.swift:22 checks !appState.isFullscreen before constructing the view it then hands isFullscreen to. Cosmetic, but it is the same drift that produced findings 3 and 6.

kept.title: Compact mode, history panel and find-again fire in every open window
kept.evidence: OraCommands posts .findNext (line 71), .findPrevious (75), .toggleCompactMode (122) and .showHistoryPanel (311) with `object: NSApp.keyWindow`, but BrowserView receives all four through plain `.onReceive(NotificationCenter.default.publisher(for:))` at lines 215, 218, 227, 230 and never looks at `notification.object`. None of these names appears in OraRoot's scoped `events` table (OraRoot.swift:377-539), which is where every other menu command is claimed by exactly one window.
kept.user_impact: With two browser windows open, ⌘B toggles compact mode in both, ⌘Y opens the history panel in both, and ⌘G steps the find in the background window's page as well as the front one. The sender is already on the notification, so the intent was per-window.
kept.fix: Give BrowserView the same test the rest of the app uses. Add `@Environment(\.window) private var window` (OraRoot already injects it at line 170) and a small helper `private func isForThisWindow(_ note: Notification) -> Bool { let sender = note.object as? NSWindow; return sender == nil || sender === window }`, then early-return from the four handlers when it is false. Leave .toggleSidebar and .toggleSidebarPosition alone: they are posted with `object: nil` on purpose.

kept.title: Stand-in traffic lights shift 2pt when a sidebar panel opens
kept.evidence: SidebarHeader pads its row `.padding(.horizontal, 12)` with the comment that this lines the stand-ins up with the native buttons (SidebarHeader.swift:93-94), and WindowAccessor places the native buttons at x = 12/32/52 (WindowAccessor.swift:21, 198). The three panel headers use `.padding(.horizontal, 10)` (HistoryPanelView.swift:95, FilesPanelView.swift:65, DownloadsHistoryView.swift:69) while their comments claim they match SidebarHeader.
kept.user_impact: With the toolbar hidden, opening history, files or downloads slides the three window buttons 2pt left, and hover-revealing the toolbar then puts the native ones 2pt right of where the stand-ins just were.
kept.fix: Change the three panel headers' leading inset to 12 to match SidebarHeader, or pad only the WindowControls block by 12 and leave the rest of the header at 10 if the 10pt inset is wanted for the panel's own content.

dropped.title: Paint probe orders two top-level windows on screen, and tiling managers re-tile the browser
dropped.reason: Refuted, the evidence is stale. AuraWebBundlePaintProbe.swift:319-323 already defines `final class HostPanel: NSPanel` overriding canBecomeKey/canBecomeMain to false and accessibilitySubrole to .floatingWindow, and hostWindow (line 325+) builds it with `[.borderless, .nonactivatingPanel]`, isFloatingPanel = true, ignoresCycle/transient collection behaviour. The doc comment above it names exactly this bug and the tiling managers it was fixed for. The auditor's proposed fix is already the shipped code; the only part not done is reparenting via addChildWindow, and a child window inherits the parent's level and would move with it, which would break the probe's requirement that each panel keeps its own visible corner.

sidebar.summary: The sidebar is in good shape structurally: the drag system is a proper AppKit dragging session with a well-documented resolver, rows share one geometry (16pt icon slot, 20pt action slot, 10pt radius), and every animation goes through AnimationSettings so reduce motion is honoured almost everywhere. The rough edges are concentrated in three places: the hover-revealed sidebar's resize handle compounds its own translation and snaps to the maximum width, the two inline rename fields (space and folder) grab focus in the same update the TextField mounts, which is exactly the pattern FindView had to defer, and the favicon path does a redundant network fetch per row for bytes already sitting on disk. There is also a measurable re-render storm: TabDragSession publishes `pointerOnRow` on every row hover, and six sidebar views observe that object, so sweeping the pointer down a tab list rebuilds the whole sidebar twice per row.

kept.title: Revealed sidebar resize handle compounds its own drag translation
kept.evidence: `ResizeHandle.onChanged` computes `max(0, min(floatingWidth + value.translation.width, totalWidth))`, but `floatingWidth` is passed in from the parent as `totalWidth * clampedFraction` where `clampedFraction = dragFraction ?? sidebarFraction.value` (lines 23-25). Each `onChanged` writes `dragFraction`, which grows `floatingWidth`, while `value.translation.width` is still measured from the gesture's start. So the base moves with the cursor and the full cumulative translation is added on top of it every frame.
kept.user_impact: Dragging the hover-revealed sidebar's edge moves it at roughly double speed and pins it at maxFraction (30%) after a few points of travel; it is effectively impossible to set an intermediate width there, and the width that gets persisted on release is wrong.
kept.fix: Capture the width the gesture started from instead of re-reading the live one: add `@State private var dragStartWidth: CGFloat?` to `ResizeHandle`, set it in `onChanged` with `let base = dragStartWidth ?? floatingWidth; dragStartWidth = base`, compute `proposedWidth` from `base`, and clear it alongside `dragFraction` in `onEnded`.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed from the code. ResizeHandle receives `floatingWidth` computed in the parent as `totalWidth * clamp(dragFraction ?? sidebarFraction.value)` (FloatingSidebarOverlay.swift:23-25), and every `onChanged` writes `dragFraction`. SwiftUI re-evaluates the GeometryReader body and re-registers the gesture's closures with the new `floatingWidth`, so the base grows while `value.translation.width` is still cumulative from the gesture start: the width roughly doubles per frame and saturates at min/maxFraction within a few points of travel. The persisted value on release is whatever it saturated at. Downgraded from high to medium: only the hover-revealed sidebar handle is affected; the docked splitter goes through HSplit/FractionHolder (BrowserSplitView.swift:42) and is unaffected.

kept.title: Space and folder rename fields take focus in the same update they mount
kept.evidence: `SpaceHeaderRow` sets `nameFieldFocused = true` inside `.onChange(of: isRenaming)`, and `FolderItem.swift:59` does the same inside `.onChange(of: isRenaming, initial: true)`. Both flips also mount the `TextField` for the first time in that same transaction. `FindView.swift:47-51` documents the opposite treatment for the same problem: "Still deferred (SwiftUI needs the window's first responder to settle first)", and defers with `DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 0.05)`.
kept.user_impact: Double-clicking a space name or choosing Rename (and creating a folder, where `createFolderForRenaming` mounts the row and arms renaming at once) sometimes shows the edit field with no caret in it, so typing goes to the window instead. Same failure the ⌘T launcher complaint describes.
kept.fix: Match FindView: wrap both assignments as `DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 0.05) { nameFieldFocused = true }`, keeping the `draftName` assignment synchronous so the field never flashes the old name.
kept.verify_reason: The code matches the description: SpaceHeaderRow.swift:65-70 sets `nameFieldFocused = true` in the same `onChange` transaction that first mounts the TextField (title(_:) branches on `isRenaming`), and FolderItem.swift:55-60 does the same with `initial: true`, which fires on the first appearance of a row created by `createFolderForRenaming` (the folder row mounts with `tabManager.renamingFolderID` already set). FindView.swift:43-51 is the codebase's own precedent and comment for exactly this problem. The failure is timing-dependent, so I cannot prove it fires every time from source alone; keeping it at medium rather than high on that basis.

kept.title: Row hover republishes TabDragSession and rebuilds the entire sidebar
kept.evidence: `@Published private(set) var pointerOnRow = false` is written from `tabDragSource`'s `.onHover { TabDragSession.shared.setPointerOnRow(id, $0) }` (TabDragSourceView.swift:368). `TabDragSession` is a plain `ObservableObject`, so any change to it invalidates every view holding `@ObservedObject private var dragSession = TabDragSession.shared`: SidebarView:25, ContainerView:19, SpaceHeaderRow:20, NormalTabsList:24, PinnedTabsList:16, FavTabsList:8. The lists use `spacing: 8`, so the pointer leaves one row before entering the next and the flag flips twice per row crossed.
kept.user_impact: Sweeping the pointer down a list of 20 tabs triggers ~40 full rebuilds of the sidebar tree (both tab lists, the favourites grid, the space header), which shows up as hover lag and wasted CPU during ordinary mousing.
kept.fix: The proposed shape is right but the code is not: `@ObservationIgnored` is an Observation-macro attribute and does not compile on an `ObservableObject`. Add a plain `@MainActor final class TabRowPointer: ObservableObject { @Published fileprivate(set) var isOnRow = false; static let shared = TabRowPointer() }` next to `TabDragSession`, move `hoveredRowID` and `setPointerOnRow` onto it, point TabDragSourceView.swift:368 at it, and have only `OraWindowDragGesture` (ContainerView.swift:169-174) observe it.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. `pointerOnRow` is @Published (TabDragSession.swift:96) and `setPointerOnRow` (lines 125-134) does dedupe, but crossing a gap between rows (lists use `spacing: 8`) genuinely flips it false then true, and each publish invalidates SidebarView:25, ContainerView:19, SpaceHeaderRow:20, NormalTabsList:24, PinnedTabsList:16, FavTabsGrid (FavTabsList.swift:8). The lists are LazyVStacks, so every visible TabItem body is re-evaluated with them. The only reader is the window-drag mask at ContainerView.swift:174.

kept.title: Every live tab row refetches its favicon over the network although the bytes are on disk
kept.evidence: `FavIcon` renders `AsyncImage(url: favicon)` whenever `isWebViewReady`, falling back to `LocalFavIcon` only as the placeholder. `Tab.setFavicon()` (Tab.swift:141-166) already downloads the icon to `faviconLocalFile`, and `FaviconService.icon(atFile:)` (FaviconService.swift:249-257) memoises the decoded image in an NSCache. `FavTabItem.swift:29` repeats the same AsyncImage branch.
kept.user_impact: Opening a window fires one HTTP request per visible tab row for an icon already stored locally, and each row visibly swaps from the disk icon to the network icon once it lands. Offline or on a slow link the rows sit on the globe placeholder even though the real icon is cached.
kept.fix: Two corrections. (1) `LocalFavIcon` hardcodes 16x16 (TabItem.swift:9-27) while FavTabItem's AsyncImage draws at 20x20, so deleting the AsyncImage branch there silently shrinks every favourite tile's icon; add a `var size: CGFloat = 16` to `LocalFavIcon` and pass 20 from FavTabItem. (2) Do not land this without sidebar-6: today the AsyncImage branch is what refreshes a visible row's icon after navigation, so removing it while `LocalFavIcon` still caches its first decode forever turns a rare stale icon into a permanent one.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. TabItem.swift:52-68 and FavTabItem.swift:29-44 both prefer `AsyncImage(url: tab.favicon)` whenever the web view is ready, with `LocalFavIcon` only as the placeholder, while `Tab.setFavicon()` (Tab.swift:130-167) already writes the icon to `faviconLocalFile` and `FaviconService.icon(atFile:)` (FaviconService.swift:247-257) memoises the decode. One network request per visible row for bytes already on disk.

kept.title: Page-hosted ContainerView subtree is missing three environment values it reads
kept.evidence: The `NSPageView` content closure re-injects six values (`tabManager`, `historyManager`, `downloadManager`, `appState`, `privacyMode`, `toolbarManager`) because, as OraRoot.swift:313-315 puts it, "views mounted inside an `NSHostingView` (the sidebar's page view) never get the window environment". The subtree also reads three values that are not injected: `ContainerView.swift:15` `@Environment(ToastManager.self)`, `TabItem.swift:102` and `FavTabItem.swift:22` `@Environment(ContainerManager.self)`, and `\.theme` (ContainerView.swift:16, TabItem.swift:106), whose `ThemeKey.defaultValue` is `Theme(colorScheme: .light)`.
kept.user_impact: Either the tab list renders with the light Theme inside a dark window, or "Move to Space" (which reads `toastManager`) and a tab's "Open in Container" submenu (which reads `containerManager.containers`) trap on a missing Observable. Adding them is correct in both cases.
kept.fix: Do not pass the captured `\.theme` value into the closure: that freezes the accent read from `@AppStorage` and re-reads the outer colorScheme. Use the existing helper instead, inside the closure, where it recomputes from the hosting view's own colorScheme: add `.withTheme()`, `.environment(toastManager)` and `.environment(containerManager)` to SidebarView.swift:301-307, plus `@Environment(ContainerManager.self) private var containerManager` on SidebarView.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed, and worse than reported. NSPageView mounts each page in a bare `NSHostingView(rootView:)` (NSPageView.swift:218-224), which starts a fresh environment; ContainerView.swift:86-90 says so in its own comment (`window` is always nil there) and SidebarView.swift:300-306 re-injects six values for that reason. `ContainerManager` is injected only at OraRoot.swift:174, above the page, so `TabItem.containerManager` (TabItem.swift:102) is missing inside the page and `containerManager.containers` is read when the row's context menu is built (auraContextMenu builds items at click time, AuraContextMenu.swift:74-76): right-clicking any pinned or normal tab row in the sidebar reads a missing Observable. `\.theme` is a custom EnvironmentKey applied once, at OraRoot.swift:190 via `.withTheme()`, so inside the page it resolves to `ThemeKey.defaultValue = Theme(colorScheme: .light)` (Theme.swift:194-196) while `\.colorScheme` is still dark (inherited via effectiveAppearance): in dark mode the tab rows draw `theme.foreground` = black on the dark sidebar. `ToastManager` (ContainerView.swift:15) is read by the Move-to-Space action. Raised to high.

kept.title: LocalFavIcon never reloads when the tab's stored favicon changes
kept.evidence: `loadFavicon` runs from `.onAppear` on the placeholder branch only, and `@State private var image` is never invalidated. Once set, the view returns early at `if let image` forever; there is no `.onChange(of: faviconLocalFile)` and no `.task(id:)`.
kept.user_impact: A row that has already drawn an icon keeps it after the tab navigates to a site with a different favicon, so a pinned or hibernated row can show the wrong site's icon until the window is rebuilt.
kept.fix: The proposed `.task(id: faviconLocalFile)` does not fire. `Tab.setFavicon` names the file `\(id.uuidString).favicon` (Tab.swift:145) and overwrites it in place, so the URL is identical across sites; on top of that `FaviconService.icon(atFile:)` keys its NSCache on the path, so it would hand back the old decode anyway. Key the reload on the thing that changes: pass `tab.favicon` down as `identity: URL?` to `LocalFavIcon`, use `.task(id: identity) { loadFavicon() }`, and drop the memoised entry when the file is rewritten (remove the path from `fileImages` in the download completion in `FaviconService.downloadAndSaveFavicon`).
kept.verify_reason: The defect is real: `LocalFavIcon.image` is @State, `loadFavicon` runs only from `.onAppear` on the globe branch (TabItem.swift:25), and once `image` is set the early return means it is never re-read. Severity lowered to low because today the AsyncImage branch masks it on every ready row; only hibernated or not-yet-ready rows show a stale icon.

kept.title: Dead pre-macOS-15 window drag backport in the sidebar
kept.evidence: `OraWindowDragGesture` branches on `if #available(macOS 15.0, *)` and otherwise uses `BackportWindowDragGesture` (lines 188-216), which drives `NSApp.keyWindow.performDrag`. `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 15.0` throughout aura.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj, so the else branch can never run. It drags `@State var isDragging` (ContainerView.swift:18), a binding, and an `Equatable` shim along with it, and the comment on line 204 ("Maybe some other case needs to be watched for here") is a note to nobody.
kept.user_impact: None at runtime; it is ~35 lines of unreachable code plus an Ora-era name in the middle of the sidebar's most subtle gesture logic, which is what makes this file hard to reason about.
kept.fix: Keep the `mask` computed property and the `#available` collapse, but note that `isDragging` (ContainerView.swift:18) is also part of the mask expression; dropping it is safe only because nothing else writes it (grep shows the binding is passed to the modifier and read nowhere else).
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed dead: `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 15.0` in all 8 build configurations of Aura.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj, so the `else` at ContainerView.swift:186-188 is unreachable, and `BackportWindowDragGesture` (188-216) with its Equatable shim and the line-204 note is dead weight. Severity is low by the stated rubric: zero runtime effect.

kept.title: Space dialogs use off-scale radii and a shadow three times the Aura elevation
kept.evidence: `NewContainerDialog` uses `.cornerRadius(11)` on the inner card, `.cornerRadius(14)` on the outer frame and `.shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.25), radius: 20, y: 8)`; `EditContainerModal.swift:32,34,41` repeats all three. Theme.swift:24-42 defines the scale (button 6, row 10, pane 13), `AuraShadow` (radius 6, y 2, opacity 0.12) and the `auraFloatingShadow()` helper, with the comment "Anything larger reads as a different elevation model next to the content pane".
kept.user_impact: The two space dialogs sit at a visibly different corner curvature and float much higher than every other floating Aura surface, which reads as a leftover from another design.
kept.fix: Keep the 3pt concentric relationship the current 11/14 encodes: inner `AuraRadius.row` (10), outer `AuraRadius.pane` (13), which the existing `.padding(3)` already matches. BookmarkEditDialog.swift:110,117,118 is a third copy of the same three values; fix it in the same pass or the inconsistency just moves.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: NewContainerButton.swift:101,109,110 and EditContainerModal.swift:32,40,41 use radius 11 / 14 and `shadow(radius: 20, y: 8, opacity 0.25)` against the scale and `auraFloatingShadow()` in Theme.swift:22-41. Severity low: two modal dialogs a user opens rarely.

kept.title: New Tab row hover is three times fainter than the tab row hover right below it
kept.evidence: `NewTabButton` uses `.interactive(cornerRadius: AuraRadius.row, tint: theme.activeTabBackground)`, whose default `hoverOpacity` is 0.10 (InteractiveButtonStyle.swift:7), so its hover fill is `activeTabBackground` at 10%. `TabItem.backgroundColor` (TabItem.swift:181-187) uses `activeTabBackground.opacity(0.3)` in dark and `0.1` in light for the same state. In dark mode that is white@1.5% against white@4.5%.
kept.user_impact: The New Tab row sits directly above the tab rows in the same list and barely lights up on hover, so it reads as disabled next to its neighbours.
kept.fix: Pass the row's own values: `.buttonStyle(InteractiveButtonStyle(cornerRadius: AuraRadius.row, hoverOpacity: colorScheme == .dark ? 0.3 : 0.1, pressOpacity: colorScheme == .dark ? 0.45 : 0.2, tint: theme.activeTabBackground))`, adding `@Environment(\.colorScheme)` to the view.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. `.interactive(cornerRadius:tint:)` (InteractiveButtonStyle.swift:47-53) does not take opacities, so NewTabButton.swift:25 gets the 0.10/0.18 defaults, while TabItem.backgroundColor (TabItem.swift:180-184) uses 0.3 dark / 0.1 light of the same tint for hover. The New Tab row sits inside the same LazyVStack as those rows (NormalTabsList.swift:63-64), so the difference is side by side.

kept.title: Reduce motion does not stop the space-switch slide
kept.evidence: `updateSelectedIndex` decides `animated` from whether a transaction animation exists (NSPageView.swift:75-77). Every space switch goes through `withAnimation(AnimationSettings.easeOut(0.1))` (SidebarView.swift:369, SpaceHeaderRow.swift:167), and with reduce motion on `AnimationSettings.easeOut` still returns a non-nil `.easeOut(duration: 0)`. So `animated` stays true and `self.animator().selectedIndex = index` runs the horizontal-strip transition at NSAnimationContext's own 0.25s default.
kept.user_impact: With Reduce Motion enabled, every other sidebar animation collapses to zero but the whole tab list still slides sideways on each space switch, which is the largest motion in the window.
kept.fix: Set the duration explicitly in the animation group: `NSAnimationContext.runAnimationGroup { ctx in ctx.duration = AnimationSettings.duration(0.25); self.animator().selectedIndex = index }`, so reduce motion zeroes it through the same helper as the rest of the chrome.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. `AnimationSettings.easeOut` returns `.easeOut(duration: 0)` under reduce motion, never nil (AnimationSettings.swift:22-24), so `animated` at NSPageView.swift:77 stays true for the space switches at SidebarView.swift:369 and SpaceHeaderRow.swift:167, and `runAnimationGroup` at NSPageView.swift:159-163 sets no duration, leaving NSAnimationContext's 0.25s horizontal strip transition.

kept.title: Space actions menu is unreachable without a pointer
kept.evidence: `menuButton` carries `.opacity(isHovering ? 1 : 0)` and `.allowsHitTesting(isHovering)`. TabItem.swift:132-136 documents the opposite decision for the same shape of control: "Hit-testable even while invisible… gating hits on `isHovering` sent that click to the row's tap gesture". The label has `.accessibilityAction` fallbacks for switching and renaming, but Change Icon, Default Container, Move Space Up/Down and Delete Space exist only behind this button.
kept.user_impact: VoiceOver and Full Keyboard Access users cannot open Space Actions at all, and a click that lands on the trailing edge in the frame before `onHover` fires falls through to the space switcher menu.
kept.fix: Same edit, different justification: drop `.allowsHitTesting(isHovering)` so the always-laid-out button behaves like the tab row's close button. Nothing else occupies that 24pt slot, so an always-hittable invisible button steals no gesture.
kept.verify_reason: The code is as described (SpaceHeaderRow.swift:134-135) and the fix is right, but the stated a11y impact is not established: VoiceOver activates through the accessibility action, not hit testing, and `.allowsHitTesting(false)` does not remove the element from the accessibility tree. What I can confirm is the click loss TabItem.swift:132-136 documents for the identical control, and the inconsistency between the two rows. Keeping it as low polish rather than medium a11y.

kept.title: Favourite tiles show only a favicon with no tooltip
kept.evidence: The tile renders a 20pt favicon and a media badge, with `.accessibilityLabel(Text(tab.title))` but no `.help(...)`. `TabItem` gets away without one because the title is on the row; `DownloadsWidget.swift:60` and `FilesWidget.swift:27` both carry `.help` for the same reason a favourite needs it.
kept.user_impact: Two favourites from the same site, or any site with a generic icon, are indistinguishable and there is no way to find out which is which short of clicking.
kept.fix: Add `.help(tab.title)` next to the existing `.accessibilityLabel` on the tile.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: the tile carries `.accessibilityLabel(Text(tab.title))` (FavTabItem.swift:103) and no `.help`, while the two other icon-only sidebar controls do (DownloadsWidget.swift:60, FilesWidget.swift:27). Cheap and correct.

kept.title: Favourite tiles resize as favourites are added
kept.evidence: `adaptiveColumns` returns `min(max(1, tabs.count), 3)` flexible `GridItem`s, so one favourite occupies the full sidebar width, two occupy half each, and a third shrinks all of them to a third. `SidebarView.swift:23` still holds the fixed `private let columns = Array(repeating: GridItem(spacing: 10), count: 3)` this replaced, now unused.
kept.user_impact: Adding a third favourite visibly resizes the two that were already there, and a single favourite renders as a 48pt full-width slab that looks nothing like the grid it belongs to.
kept.fix: Hardcoding three columns breaks the empty state: with `tabs.isEmpty` the grid currently has one column, which is what makes `EmptyFavTabItem` and the invisible `emptyHotStrip` drop target span the sidebar (FavTabsList.swift:31-45). Return three columns only when `!tabs.isEmpty`, or keep three always and put `.gridCellColumns(3)` on both empty-state branches.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: `adaptiveColumns` (FavTabsList.swift:20-24) returns `min(max(1, tabs.count), 3)` flexible columns and `FavTabItem` is `.frame(height: 48).frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` (FavTabItem.swift:83-84), so one favourite is a full-width 48pt slab and adding a third resizes the first two. `SidebarView.swift:23 columns` is indeed unused.

kept.title: Dead state, dead environment reads and an unused parameter across the sidebar
kept.evidence: `SidebarView.swift:23` `columns` and `:30` `isHoveringSidebarToggle` are never read (grep of the file shows single occurrences). `ContainerView.swift:9` declares `@Environment(AppState.self) private var appState`, never used, and SidebarView injects `appState` into the page closure only to feed it. `ContainerForm.swift:11` takes `let defaultEmoji: String`, never referenced in the body, and both call sites pass `ContainerConstants.defaultEmoji`.
kept.user_impact: None at runtime; it keeps a live environment dependency and a parameter alive that suggest behaviour that does not exist, which is what makes the sidebar read as unfinished.
kept.fix: `defaultEmoji` has three call sites, not two: NewContainerButton.swift:68, EditContainerModal.swift:68 and Onboarding/OnboardingSteps.swift:319 — add that file to files_to_touch or the build breaks. Also keep `.environment(appState)` in SidebarView's page closure: `SidebarURLDisplay` is mounted by ContainerView and reads it (SidebarURLDisplay.swift:6,18-20); only ContainerView's own unused property goes.
kept.verify_reason: All four confirmed by grep: `columns` and `isHoveringSidebarToggle` occur once each in SidebarView.swift (:23, :30), ContainerView.swift:9 `appState` occurs once, and `ContainerForm.defaultEmoji` (ContainerForm.swift:11) is never referenced in the form body.

kept.title: Tab rows have hover and selected states but no pressed state
kept.evidence: The row activates through `.onTapGesture { onTap() }`, and `backgroundColor` (lines 176-189) covers dragging, selected and hovering only. Every button in the sidebar goes through `InteractiveButtonStyle`, which explicitly adds a `pressOpacity` step (InteractiveButtonStyle.swift:33) with the note "The press tint is the feedback". `FavTabItem.swift:159-168` has the same gap.
kept.user_impact: Clicking a tab gives no feedback until the page swaps, so a click on a slow-waking hibernated tab feels like it was missed. It is the one control in the sidebar that does not answer the mouse down.
kept.fix: Guard the interaction with the drag machinery before shipping it. The row's drag is armed by a global NSEvent monitor that passes `.leftMouseDown`/`.leftMouseDragged` through to SwiftUI and swallows only the event that starts the drag (TabDragSourceView.swift:59-83), so a `DragGesture(minimumDistance: 0)` will fire but its `@GestureState` may not reset when the AppKit drag session takes over. Clear the tint when `dragSession.draggedID == tab.id` as well, or drive the press state from `TabDragSourceRegistry`'s existing pressed-row bookkeeping instead of adding a second gesture.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed gap: the row activates on `.onTapGesture` (TabItem.swift:158) and `backgroundColor` (176-189) has no pressed branch, while every button in the sidebar gets one from InteractiveButtonStyle.swift:33. FavTabItem.swift:163-172 is the same. Low: cosmetic feedback only.

kept.title: Sidebar pages keep the space list they were built with
kept.evidence: `makeNSViewController` captures the content closure once (`controller.objectToView = { object in contentView(object) }`, NSPageView.swift:46-48) and `NSPageViewContentController` builds its `NSHostingView` once, in `viewDidLoad` (NSPageView.swift:211-227). `updateNSViewController` (NSPageView.swift:69-90) only refreshes `pageObjects`, the data source and the selected index; it never reassigns `objectToView` and never touches an existing page's `rootView`. SidebarView passes the live `@Query` result into that closure as `ContainerView(container:containers:)` (SidebarView.swift:294-297), and `containers` is forwarded down to every row as `availableContainers` (NormalTabsList.swift:22, TabItem.swift:99).
kept.user_impact: Create or delete a space and the sidebar header updates (it is outside the page view) while the tab rows inside it do not: a tab's "Move to Space" and "Open in Space" submenus keep listing the old set, so a new space is missing and a deleted one is still offered, and picking the deleted one calls `moveTabToContainer` with a container that no longer exists.
kept.fix: In `updateNSViewController`, inside the existing `pageObjects != pageObjects` branch, reassign `controller.objectToView = { contentView($0) }` and add a `refreshContent()` on `NSPageViewContainerController` that walks `children.compactMap { $0 as? NSPageViewContentController<T, V> }` and re-sets `hostingView.rootView = AnyView(content(object).ignoresSafeArea())`. Scoping it to that branch keeps row `@State` (hover, rename drafts) intact for the common case where only the selection changed.

kept.title: pointerOnRow can stay latched after the hovered row disappears
kept.evidence: `hoveredRowID` is only ever written from `.onHover` on the row (TabDragSourceView.swift:368) and cleared only by that same row reporting `false`. TabItem.swift:132-136 records that after a close "the next row slides under a stationary pointer, `onHover` does not re-fire", and `TabDragSourceAnchor.dismantleNSView` (TabDragSourceView.swift:337-339) unregisters the drag source without touching the session. So closing the row under the pointer can leave `hoveredRowID` pointing at a tab that no longer exists.
kept.user_impact: With the flag latched, `OraWindowDragGesture`'s mask stays `.subviews` (ContainerView.swift:174) and dragging the window by the sidebar background stops working until the pointer enters and leaves another row.
kept.fix: Clear the flag when the row goes away: give `tabDragSource` an `.onDisappear { TabDragSession.shared.setPointerOnRow(id, false) }` next to the existing `.onHover`, which reuses the id-guarded clear already in `setPointerOnRow`.

extensions-scripts.summary: The extension stack is unusually well thought through for a WebKit browser: the shim, the relay and the injected-bundle broker carry their reasoning in comments and most of the pure logic is covered by tests. The real damage is concentrated in two places that both fire on ordinary launches: the paint probe puts two floating NSWindows on screen every time the app starts with default settings, and a shim version bump rewrites an MV3 service worker into a file that imports itself. Past that it is rough edges rather than breakage: installs unpack tens of megabytes on the main actor, a failed update check wipes every pending offer, removing an extension purges its storage with no confirmation, and the extension toolbar buttons have no loading state and no accessibility labels.

kept.title: A shim version bump rewrites an MV3 service worker into a file that imports itself
kept.evidence: `apply(at:)` reads the manifest on disk and passes it straight to `patchedBackground(manifest["background"] …)` (line 81). On a re-patch (`manifest[versionKey] == 6` while `version == 7`) that on-disk manifest is the patched one, so `background["service_worker"]` is already `"aura-shim-worker.js"`. `patchedBackground` then writes `files = prelude + [worker]` into `aura-shim-worker.js`, producing `importScripts('aura-shim-manifest.js', 'aura-shim.js', 'aura-shim-worker.js');` — the wrapper importing itself — and the author's real worker filename is gone from the manifest for good. The two sibling shapes are guarded (`scripts` does `scripts.removeAll(where: prelude.contains)` at line 200, the `page` branch by `!html.contains(scriptName)` at line 241), and line 79 already reads `pristineManifest(in:)` for the manifest script, so this branch is the one that was missed. `WebRequestBrokerTests.shimWrapsAServiceWorkerAndABackgroundPage` only patches a fresh folder, so nothing catches it.
kept.user_impact: After an Aura update that bumps `ExtensionShim.version`, every installed MV3 extension with a service worker (most current AMO/Chrome add-ons) stops running: the background never executes, the popup is blank, and reinstalling is the only way back.
kept.fix: Patch the background the author shipped, not the one on disk: in `apply`, `let base = pristineManifest(in: directory) ?? manifest` and call `patchedBackground(base["background"] as? [String: Any], in: directory)` — the same source `writeManifestScript` uses one line above. Add a case to `shimWrapsAServiceWorkerAndABackgroundPage` that applies twice across a version bump and expects `importScripts(… 'sw.js')`.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. ExtensionShim.apply passes the on-disk manifest to `patchedBackground` (ExtensionShim.swift:81) while the sibling manifest script one line above deliberately reads `pristineManifest(in:) ?? manifest` (line 79). On a re-patch (`manifest[versionKey] as? Int != version`, gate at line 57) `background["service_worker"]` is already `aura-shim-worker.js`, so line 205 writes `importScripts('aura-shim-manifest.js', 'aura-shim.js', 'aura-shim-worker.js');` into that same file. The `scripts` branch (line 200) and the `page` branch (via `!html.contains(scriptName)`, line 241) are both guarded; only this one is not. Trigger is a bump of `ExtensionShim.version` (currently 7), i.e. the next Aura release that touches the shim, and every installed MV3 add-on with a service worker breaks silently at that launch. One correction to the evidence: the author's worker filename is not lost for good, `aura-shim-original-manifest` still holds it, so the patched fix recovers the folder without a reinstall. An add-on update does not trigger it (`replaceContents` wipes the folder, so the next patch sees a pristine manifest with `versionKey == nil`).

kept.title: A one-shot runtime.sendMessage never settles when the background page goes away
kept.evidence: `relaySendMessage` (aura-shim.js:403) files a `relayReplies` entry per portId and returns a promise that only resolves on an `op: 'response'` frame; there is no timeout. On the host, `backgroundDidDisconnect` sends `["op": "disconnect", "portId": portID]` to each owner page, and the shim's `onRelayFrame` `case 'disconnect'` returns early when `relayPorts.get(portId)` is undefined — which it always is for a one-shot, because `relaySendMessage` never calls `makeRelayPort`. The broadcast direction was given exactly this care (line 120 answers `NSNull()` itself when no page is open); the page-to-background direction was not. `sendToBackground` has the same hole: with no background port the frame is queued up to `queueLimit` and silently dropped if the background never attaches.
kept.user_impact: An extension whose background page crashes or is torn down leaves every open popup spinning forever with no error, which is the classic stuck extension popup.
kept.fix: As proposed, plus flush the parked queue in the same place: `queued.removeValue(forKey:)` at ExtensionMessageRelay.swift:191 already drops frames whose promises are still pending on the page side, so answer those portIds with the same null `response` before dropping them.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed on both sides. aura-shim.js:403-412 registers the one-shot resolver in `relayReplies` with no timeout and never calls `makeRelayPort`, so `relayPorts.get(portId)` is undefined and `onRelayFrame`'s `case 'disconnect'` (line 373-377) returns before touching `relayReplies`. `backgroundDidDisconnect` (ExtensionMessageRelay.swift:190-196) sends only the `disconnect` frame, while the mirror-image no-page case answers `op: 'response'` with `NSNull()` itself (line 120). The proposed fix is safe: a real tunnelled port ignores a `response` frame whose portId is not in `relayReplies`, and a one-shot ignores the `disconnect`.

kept.title: Installing an add-on unpacks and copies tens of megabytes on the main actor
kept.evidence: `ExtensionManager` is `@MainActor`, and `installArchive(at:source:)` calls `XPIUnpacker.unpack` (which runs `/usr/bin/ditto` and blocks on `readDataToEndOfFile` + `waitUntilExit`) then `installExtension(from:)`, whose `try FileManager.default.copyItem(at: sourceURL, to: destination)` (line 572) copies the whole unpacked folder. Every install path lands there on the actor: `installFirefoxAddon` (line 587), `installExtension(fromFile:)` (lines 607 and 613). `updateExtension` already does the identical work off the actor in `Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated)` (ExtensionManager+Updates.swift:79).
kept.user_impact: Pressing Install in the store or picking a file freezes every window and tab for a second or more on a large add-on such as uBlock Origin.
kept.fix: Same shape as the update path, but keep the signatures synchronous-friendly: leave the duplicate check, `finishScanNow()` and `registerExtension` on the actor and move only unpack+copy into `try await Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated) { ... }.value`. files_to_touch must also include aura/Features/Settings/Sections/ExtensionsSettingsView.swift, whose `promptForFile` (line 92) calls the same method and needs the same `Task { }` wrap.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. `ExtensionManager` is `@Observable @MainActor` (ExtensionManager.swift:75), `installArchive` runs `XPIUnpacker.unpack` and `installExtension(from:)`'s `copyItem` inline on the actor (lines 617-625, 572), and the update path does the identical work in `Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated)` (ExtensionManager+Updates.swift:79-84) with a comment saying why. Callers correction: `installExtension(fromFile:)` is called from two views, ExtensionStoreView.swift:206 and ExtensionsSettingsView.swift:104, not one.

kept.title: A failed update check throws away every update offer and parks the next check for a day
kept.evidence: `ExtensionUpdates.check` swallows every per-extension failure (`guard let addon = try? await fetch(geckoID)` … `continue`) and returns `[:]` when AMO is unreachable. `adoptUpdateCheck` then does `SettingsStore.shared.extensionUpdateLastCheck = Date()` and `SettingsStore.shared.extensionAvailableUpdates = found` unconditionally, with a comment claiming the wholesale replace keeps stale offers away. `ExtensionUpdates.isDue` then refuses another check for 24 h.
kept.user_impact: Launch once offline and every "Update to x.y" button disappears for a day, so the user never learns their add-ons are out of date.
kept.fix: Smaller than the proposed API change: keep the return type and add a second value, or simplest, have `check` return `nil` only when it fetched nothing successfully. Whichever shape, the load-bearing edit is the guard in `adoptUpdateCheck` so neither `extensionUpdateLastCheck` nor `extensionAvailableUpdates` moves on a check that reached nobody.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: `ExtensionUpdates.check` returns `[:]` when every fetch throws (ExtensionUpdates.swift:65-75) and `adoptUpdateCheck` stamps `extensionUpdateLastCheck` and overwrites `extensionAvailableUpdates` unconditionally (ExtensionManager+Updates.swift:47-50), with `isDue` then blocking the automatic check for 24 h. The auto check runs from `adoptScan` at every launch (ExtensionManager.swift:288), so one offline launch clears every stored offer and the Update buttons vanish from the store rows. Impact is softer than stated: Settings > Extensions has a "Check for updates" button that passes `force: true` (ExtensionsSettingsView.swift:54), so the state is recoverable by hand.

kept.title: The trash button deletes an extension and all its stored data with no confirmation
kept.evidence: `ExtensionRemoveButton`'s action is `ExtensionManager.shared.removeExtension(id)` with nothing in between, and that call deletes the folder, runs `purgeStoredData(for:)` (`controller.removeData(ofTypes:from:)` over `allExtensionDataTypes`), and clears the consent record, the private-window grant, the update offer and every custom shortcut. The button sits a few points from the enable switch in both the store card (line 102) and the installed row (line 214), and there is no undo.
kept.user_impact: One stray click on a small icon permanently destroys a password manager's settings or uBlock Origin's whole filter configuration.
kept.fix: Do not hand-build a sheet: `DialogManager` already has `confirm(title:message:icon:confirmLabel:variant:onConfirm:...)` (DialogManager.swift:48). Take `@Environment(DialogManager.self)` in `ExtensionRemoveButton`, pass the display name in beside the id, and call `dialogManager.confirm(title: "Remove \(name)?", message: "Its settings and stored data are deleted.", confirmLabel: "Remove", variant: .destructive) { ExtensionManager.shared.removeExtension(id) }`.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed: `ExtensionRemoveButton` (ExtensionStoreCards.swift:262-278) calls `removeExtension(id)` straight from the button action, and that method deletes the folder, purges WebKit storage, and clears consent, private-window grant, update offer and shortcuts (ExtensionManager.swift:650+). It sits 6 pt from the enable toggle in both the store card (line 102) and the installed row (line 214), with no undo. Both call sites live in `ExtensionStoreView`, which renders inside the browser window under `OraRoot`'s `.environment(dialogManager)` (OraRoot.swift:186), so the dialog stack is reachable.

kept.title: Extension toolbar buttons look live before their extension has loaded and do nothing when clicked
kept.evidence: `ExtensionToolbarIcons` renders a button for every row with `isEnabled == true`, and rows exist from the folder scan onwards, well before `performLoad` finishes parsing the extension and compiling its rules. `ExtensionManager.performAction` (ExtensionManager.swift:384) documents the outcome itself — "Silence here looks like a dead button, so at least the log says which of those it was" — then returns after logging when `engine.context(for:)` is nil. The same button stays fully opaque when the row carries a `loadError` or is waiting on consent (`awaitingConsentNote`).
kept.user_impact: For the first seconds of every launch, and permanently for an extension that failed to load, the toolbar shows normal-looking extension buttons whose clicks are silently ignored.
kept.fix: Use `loadedEngine` in the accessor exactly as `actionIcon`/`actionBadgeText` do (ExtensionManager.swift:405, 410) so readiness never forces the engine into existence, and drop the `.help(item.loadError ?? item.displayName)` swap for a fallback that keeps the name: `.help(item.loadError.map { "\(item.displayName): \($0)" } ?? item.displayName)`, since a bare error string with no extension name is worse than the current tooltip.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed. `ExtensionToolbarIcons` filters only on `isEnabled` (TopToolbar.swift:377), rows exist from the scan, and `performAction` logs and returns when `engine.context(for:)` is nil (ExtensionManager.swift:387-398). The permanent case is real, not just the launch window: `loadIntoEngine` parks a row on `awaitingConsentNote` while still enabled (ExtensionManager+Loading.swift:80-88), and a `loadError` row stays enabled too, so those buttons are dead for the whole session. The `.disabled` will actually flip when the load lands, because `performLoad` mutates the row through `update(id:)` (ExtensionManager+Loading.swift:173) and the row is observed.

kept.title: The additional-access prompt is a stock NSAlert listing raw manifest keys
kept.evidence: `requestAdditionalAccess` builds an `NSAlert` whose `informativeText` is `permissions.sorted().joined(separator: "\n")`, so the user reads `*://*.example.com/*` or `webRequestBlocking`. The install-time sheet next door renders the same data through `ExtensionConsentRequest.permissionLines`, which maps each entry with `ExtensionCompatibility.humanPermission` ("Read and change data on example.com"), de-duplicates, and draws it in Aura's own flat dialog with `auraFloatingShadow()` and the `AuraRadius` scale.
kept.user_impact: The one permission decision made mid-session looks like a system error dialog and asks about strings a user cannot evaluate, while the install decision is a designed sheet in plain English.
kept.fix: Do only the wording half. Lift the four lines of `permissionLines` into `static func humanPermissionLines(_ raw: [String]) -> [String]` on `ExtensionCompatibility`, call it from both `permissionLines` and `requestAdditionalAccess`, and leave the NSAlert in place; replacing a sheet-modal alert with a `DialogManager` dialog would have to re-plumb the `completionHandler` and is not worth the size for this path.
kept.verify_reason: Code confirmed: `requestAdditionalAccess` joins raw permission strings into an `NSAlert.informativeText` (ExtensionControllerDelegate.swift:118-122), while the install sheet renders the same data through `permissionLines` -> `ExtensionCompatibility.humanPermission` (ExtensionEngine.swift:53-58, ExtensionCompatibility.swift:177). Downgraded to low: this delegate only fires for a runtime optional-permission or match-pattern request, which most installed add-ons never make, so it is not something a user meets in a normal session. The wording half of the fix is worth doing on its own.

kept.title: Extension enable switches and the remove button carry no accessibility label
kept.evidence: Both enable toggles are `Toggle("", isOn: …).toggleStyle(.switch).labelsHidden()` (lines 94 and 207), so their accessibility label is the empty string; `.help("Disable")` on the store card supplies help text, not a name, and the installed row has no `.help` at all. `ExtensionRemoveButton` is an unlabelled `Image(systemName: "trash")` with only `.help("Remove extension")`. The toolbar buttons in the same feature do it correctly (`.accessibilityLabel(Text(item.displayName))`, TopToolbar.swift:412).
kept.user_impact: With VoiceOver the extensions list reads as a run of anonymous switches and buttons, so there is no way to tell which extension is being disabled or deleted.
kept.fix: Give each control a real label without changing the layout: `Toggle("Enable \(item.displayName)", isOn: …).labelsHidden()` in both places (labelsHidden keeps the label for assistive tech), and on `ExtensionRemoveButton` add `.accessibilityLabel(Text("Remove \(name)"))` with the name passed in beside the id, which the confirmation in extensions-scripts-6 needs anyway.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed by reading both controls: the store card toggle (ExtensionStoreCards.swift:94-101) and the installed-row toggle (line 207-212) are `Toggle("", ...)` with `.labelsHidden()`, and `ExtensionRemoveButton` (line 262-278) is a bare `Image(systemName: "trash")` with `.help` only. `.help` maps to the AX help attribute, not the title, so VoiceOver announces "switch" and "button" with no name. TopToolbar.swift:412-413 shows the pattern the same feature uses correctly.

kept.title: A multi-digit action badge spills over the neighbouring toolbar icon
kept.evidence: The badge is `Text(text) … .fixedSize().offset(x: 4, y: -2)` in an `.overlay(alignment: .topTrailing)`, with no `lineLimit` or width cap, and the icon row is an `HStack(spacing: 2)`. `browser.action.setBadgeText` may set four or five characters (uBlock Origin puts a blocked-request count there), and `fixedSize` lets the capsule grow past the 4-point offset into the next button. `setBadgeBackgroundColor` is ignored too: the fill is always `theme.accent`.
kept.user_impact: With a blocker showing a count the badge overlaps the next extension icon and the toolbar row looks broken on busy pages.
kept.fix: The proposed `.frame(maxWidth: 22)` has no effect while `.fixedSize()` is on the same `Text`. Drop `.fixedSize()`, then add `.lineLimit(1)` and `.frame(maxWidth: 22, alignment: .center)`. Clamping in `liveBadgeText()` is still the cheap half: `text.count > 4 ? "999+" : text`.
kept.verify_reason: Confirmed as written: the badge `Text` has `.fixedSize()`, no `lineLimit`, no width cap, and sits in an `.overlay(alignment: .topTrailing)` offset 4 pt outward inside an `HStack(spacing: 2)` (TopToolbar.swift:444-455). `actionBadgeText` passes whatever the extension set (ExtensionManager.swift:409-413), and uBO-style counters do run to four or five characters. The accent-only fill is also real (`setBadgeBackgroundColor` is never read), though that is cosmetic.

kept.title: Dead consent branch and a comment that contradicts the code in Privacy settings
kept.evidence: The comment reads "Full uBlock Origin installs from the switch above, and it is not pre-consented, so this section has to be able to show the sheet", but `BundledExtensions.preConsentedIDs` contains `FullUBlockOrigin.folderName` (BundledExtensions.swift:39) and `blockingInputs()` hardcodes `fullConsented: true` and `fullConsentRecorded: true` (lines 319-320). `plan(for:)` can therefore never return `pending == .consent` in the app, so the `.consent` case of `waitingMessage` (line 130), the `.extensionConsentPrompt()` at line 45 and the `onChange(of: pendingConsent.isEmpty)` at line 48 are reachable only from tests. `SettingsStore.swift:177` repeats the same stale claim ("Off by default, and not pre-consented") about a setting line 443 defaults to `true`.
kept.user_impact: Nothing visible, but the next person changing the blocker rule reads three comments describing a consent flow the shipping build does not have.
kept.fix: Comments only. Do not delete the `.extensionConsentPrompt()` at PrivacySettingsView.swift:45 or the `.consent` case in `waitingMessage`: the modifier costs nothing, `pending` is a public enum `plan(for:)` still returns in tests, and `apply(_:)` branches on `plan.pending != .consent` (BundledExtensions.swift:413), so the case is load-bearing in the model even though the settings tab cannot reach it. Rewrite the two comments to say full uBO is pre-consented like Lite.
